A_target.statement:
Let $\Sigma$ be a set of propositional formulas in the variables $p_1, p_2, \ldots$.
If every finite subset of $\Sigma$ is [[Definition:Satisfiable|satisfiable]], then $\Sigma$ is satisfiable.

B_source.statement: Every infinite [[Definition:Rooted Tree|rooted tree]] in which every vertex has finitely many children has an infinite [[Definition:Path (Graph Theory)|path]] from the root.

substitutions.the tree: partial truth assignments to p_1, ..., p_n falsifying no formula over those variables

object_map.reformulation: Arrange the good partial assignments in a binary tree and extract an infinite branch.

validity_conditions: Formulas over p_1, ..., p_n express only finitely many truth functions, so finite satisfiability makes each level non-empty.
Restricting a good assignment to fewer variables keeps it good, so the nodes form a tree.
proof_plan:
Let the nodes at level $n$ be the assignments $v: \set {p_1, \ldots, p_n} \to \set {0, 1}$ falsifying no formula of $\Sigma$ whose variables lie among $p_1, \ldots, p_n$.
Restriction to $\set {p_1, \ldots, p_{n - 1} }$ gives the parent, so this is a tree with at most two children per node.

The formulas of $\Sigma$ in $p_1, \ldots, p_n$ express finitely many truth functions, so a finite subset of them is equivalent to all of them.
By hypothesis that finite subset is satisfiable, so level $n$ is non-empty and the tree is infinite.
By [[König's Lemma]], there is an infinite branch, which defines a total assignment $v$.
